statement: In one Colorado field study of 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month (55 using flower, 66 using concentrates; each person chose the form, and a labelled strength was assigned at random within each form), blood THC measured about 13 minutes after they used their own product in their own way at home was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and so was the active by-product 11-OH-THC, at every time point including before use. Even so, self-rated intoxication (form effect P = .11) and the marijuana effects scale (P = .18) did not differ by form, tension and vigor ratings were lower in the concentrate group, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. Delayed verbal recall worsened after use in both groups (form effect P = .65), and eyes-closed balance worsened and was back at its pre-use level by one hour in both (form effect P = .85); the main text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form at its set threshold (P < .01), with the strength tests in a supplement that was not read. The authors offer three untested explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, individual differences) and read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within a form as suggesting that people adjust how much they take. The groups were not alike before the session: the concentrate group had used concentrates on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, had begun regular use at 17.7 years against 20.0 and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite, and it used about half as much product by weight at the session. There was no placebo or no-use session, so changes after use cannot be told apart from repeating the tests; follow-up was one hour; form was not randomised, so earlier differences between the groups may account for some findings; 12 of the 133 people assessed were left out because blood THC after use was very low (9 of 64 on flower, 3 of 69 on concentrates; editors' arithmetic from the group sizes); and people had to have used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction and to use no other drugs or daily tobacco, so the findings do not reach people who use cannabis rarely, are new to it, or do not use it. Tobacco mixed into joints was not recorded and cannabinoids other than THC were not reported. The authors' Conclusions voice concern about long-term effects, which were not measured, and the Abstract and Results print the spread of blood THC as standard errors although the Discussion gives standard deviations. A scoping review done for the State of Colorado searched seven databases to mid-2022 and mapped 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product (225 observational studies, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% published 2017 to 2022). Only 54 (12%) examined concentrates and a health outcome directly and 189 (42%) examined THC concentration directly; 63% studied generic cannabis types, and products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, resins) were examined in about 2% to 10% of studies. The median strength studied was 12% THC where given as a percentage (15 mg where given in milligrams), well below the Colorado market strengths the authors cite from other sources for 2020 (flower averaging 19%, concentrates 68%), which they think likely reflects the restriction of research cannabis to a federal supply without concentrates. Only 47% of studies had a control group and 41% reported effect estimates, and most did not capture the elements of use needed to estimate exposure. The review extracted no study results and did not assess bias, so it shows what has been studied and not what was found; its Conclusions say the literature has serious limits in generalisability to the current market and that high-quality evidence bearing on whether to regulate THC concentration is scarce. Searches were English-only, designed to be sensitive rather than specific, and screened with AI assistance, so studies may be missing; the evidence map and the appendix were not read. Of the 452 studies, 25 (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author with a disclosed industry tie, while 24% reported no funding source and 32% no conflict statement. Nothing read here compares people who use concentrates with people who do not use cannabis, follows anyone beyond one hour, or reports long-term, lung, dependence or mental-health results for concentrates. Funding as printed: the field study, the US National Institutes of Health and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, with the paper stating that the funders had no role in the study; participants bought their products at one local dispensary that set aside allotments for the study, with no payment declared; the review, the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317 (funder not involved), with authors' interests as printed (a paid consultancy for Health Canada on conflict of interest, a paid UpToDate chapter, research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research and a seat on the state health department's marijuana advisory committee). No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed for either paper.
plain: In one Colorado study, 121 adults who already used cannabis regularly used their own flower or their own concentrate (a strong extract of cannabis, such as wax or shatter) at home while researchers took blood and ran memory and balance tests. People who used concentrates had more THC in their blood than people who used flower, but they did not rate themselves as more intoxicated, and the memory and balance tests changed in similar ways in both groups. The two groups were not alike to begin with (the concentrate group already used concentrates much more often), nobody had a dummy dose, and people were followed for only an hour, so the study cannot show that concentrates are more or less impairing than flower, or what happens with longer use, and it did not include people who do not use cannabis. A separate review for the state of Colorado found 452 studies that report THC strength, but only 54 looked at concentrates and a health outcome directly; its authors say the strengths studied are well below those now sold, and the review did not check how good the studies were or report what they found.
population: 121 adults in Colorado (mean age about 28; 42% to 48% women) who used cannabis at least four times a month, had used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction, and used no other non-prescription drugs or daily tobacco (Bidwell 2020); and 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product, 1971 to 2022 (Bero 2023, scoping review).
exposure: Concentrates (laboratory-tested, labelled 70% or 90% THC, assigned at random within the form; the form itself self-chosen), used in the person's usual way at home (glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%) in one session after 5 days of free use (study conditions only); in the review, studies of concentrates or other high-concentration products and of THC concentration.
comparator: Flower (labelled 16% or 24% THC; pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%) in a separate group of regular consumers who chose flower; no placebo or no-use session, and no people who do not use cannabis. In the review, no comparison of outcomes (an inventory of studies).
outcome: Blood THC and 11-OH-THC, self-rated intoxication and marijuana-effects scale, mood (tension, vigor), delayed verbal recall, inhibitory control and working memory, and balance, before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. In the review, counts of studies by exposure, outcome, design and reporting.
magnitude: Field study (Bidwell 2020), concentrate group (n = 66) against flower group (n = 55), means before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use. Blood THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. 11-OH-THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; form effect P < .001. Self-rated intoxication (scale range inconsistently described in the paper): concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; form effect P = .11. Marijuana effects scale: form effect P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01 and P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; change after use P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Eyes-closed sway: concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001). Thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold of P < .01; no placebo. Baseline, concentrate against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 vs 3.5 of the past 30 days; regular use begun at 17.7 vs 20.0 years; THC-COOH 0.087 vs 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g vs 0.22 g (study measure only). Labelled strengths assigned at random within form: flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90% THC; groups of 26 to 33 people. 133 assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 left out for post-use blood THC below 0.02 µg/mL (9 flower, 3 concentrate). Scoping review (Bero 2023): 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full texts, 452 studies (225 observational, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series); 54 (12%) concentrates and an outcome directly, 189 (42%) THC concentration and an outcome directly, 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) indirectly; control group in 212 (47%); effect estimates in 184 (41%); generic cannabis types in 284 (63%); products typically high in concentration in about 2% to 10%; THC given as a percentage in 172 studies, median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%), and in milligrams in 113, median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26); market strengths cited by the authors from other sources for Colorado: flower averaging 14% (2014) to 19% (2020), concentrates 46% to 68%. Funding of the included studies: 25 (6%) cannabis industry, 58 (13%) author with an industry tie, 109 (24%) no funding source reported, 143 (32%) no conflict statement. Outcome domains most studied: mental health 40%, neurologic 30%, pain 29%, cardiometabolic 24%, gastrointestinal 22%, psychosocial 22%, sleep 21%.

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Experimental Appointment, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Adults aged 21 to 70 who had used cannabis at least four times in the past month and had used, at least once, the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days, no daily tobacco, light alcohol use. Within each form, participants were randomly assigned by random-number table to a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), bought it at a local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study, used it freely for 5 days, and on the fifth day used it in their preferred way at home before a mobile-laboratory visit; measures were taken before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. The form itself was each person's own choice.

evidence.locator: Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Abstract; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 133 people were assessed (64 in the flower group, 69 in the concentrate group). Twelve were excluded because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24), taken to mean they had not used the product at home as instructed, leaving 121 (55 flower, 66 concentrate, so 9 and 3 were left out from the two groups; editors' arithmetic); mean age 28.8 and 28.3 years; 42% and 48% women in Table 1 (the Abstract gives 46% and 45%). Table 1: concentrate group glass rig or tube 92% and hash pen 8%; flower group pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%.

THC and 11-OH-THC peaked at the short-term post-use assessment and then fell. Mean blood THC after use was 0.32 µg/mL in the concentrate group and 0.14 µg/mL in the flower group (printed as SE 0.43 and 0.16 in the Abstract and Results; the Discussion gives them as standard deviations). THC and 11-OH-THC were consistently higher in the concentrate group across assessments, including before use (Table 2, THC 0.01, 0.32, 0.03 against 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; 11-OH-THC 0.004, 0.011, 0.008 against 0.001, 0.005, 0.004 µg/mL); form effect for THC F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. The text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form on blood levels.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Self-rated intoxication, the marijuana effects scale, tension and vigor peaked at the short-term assessment and decreased by 1 hour. Intoxication did not differ by form (form effect P = .11; means 0.08, 2.40, 1.93 in the flower group and 0.14, 2.35, 1.63 in the concentrate group); the marijuana effects scale did not differ by form (P = .18); tension (P < .01) and vigor (P < .001) were lower in the concentrate group across assessments. No associations with labelled strength are reported in the main text.

evidence.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Cognition, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: Delayed verbal recall errors rose after use in both groups (linear effect P < .001; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33 before, short-term and 1 hour after); form effect P = .65, form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session, which the authors suggest may reflect practice; inhibitory control was higher in the flower group across all assessments, with no short-term change and no association with labelled strength.

evidence.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Balance, paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Eyes-closed sway rose after use and returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour in both groups (quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85). Eyes-open balance showed a trend (P = .05) that did not meet the a priori threshold; the eyes-closed head-back condition showed no change from before to after use. The authors describe about an 11% increase in sway with eyes closed, which they say is consistent with effects of moderate alcohol (as cited).

evidence.locator: Table 1; Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: At baseline, concentrate group against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 against 3.5 of the past 30 days; flower use on 15.4 against 20.6 days; regular use begun at 17.7 against 20.0 years; baseline THC-COOH 0.087 against 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g against 0.22 g. Between the two strength groups within each form there were no differences except in race among the concentrate groups (P < .01), and none in the amount used.

The authors write that there was no within-form association of labelled strength with blood levels, suggesting that people may titrate toward similar THC exposure as strength rises. For similar intoxication despite higher blood THC they offer greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, and individual differences in metabolism or sensitivity, and say future research must test them.

Ethical limits precluded random assignment to concentrate or flower, so pre-existing differences between the groups may partially account for the findings; there was no placebo control because such products do not exist on the legal market; federal rules restricted control over dosing and masking to product strength; interactions of cannabinoid strength and ratio, mode of use, expectancies and technique were not tested.

Delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; people who used concentrates showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than people who used flower; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications. The Key Points say concentrates were associated with higher THC exposure and potentially greater risk. Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.

evidence.locator: Author-information panel (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor); Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding: NIH grant DA039707 (Hutchison) and Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment grant 96947 (Bidwell); the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit. Disclosures: Bidwell reports grants from NIH/NIDA and the State of Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment; Ellingson NIH; Klawitter the department and NIH; Sempio the department and NIH; Bryan NIH and the State of Colorado; no other disclosures. Participants bought their assigned products at one local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study; no payment from the dispensary is declared.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data Sources and Searches
evidence.extracted: Seven databases were searched (October 2021, updated July 2022; English language and human studies only) for human studies of any design that reported a THC concentration in any unit or a product from which a high concentration could be inferred. Searches identified 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports and 452 included studies: 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series. The earliest was published in 1971 and 60% (269) in 2017 to 2022.

evidence.locator: Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 452 studies, 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome and 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome; 114 (25%) examined an indirect association between THC concentration and outcomes and 62 (14%) an indirect association between concentrates and outcomes; 212 (47%) had a control group; effect estimates were reported in 184 (41%), measures of precision in 274 (61%), significance tests in 335 (74%) and raw data in 232 (51%).

Most studies concerned generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies. When THC was given as a percentage (172 studies, 349 exposures) the median was 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%); when given in milligrams (113 studies, 143 exposures) the median was 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Units and indices varied.

Market strengths the authors cite from other sources: a 2018 survey of products sold in 7 US states found most products between 15% and 30% THC; in Colorado the average THC of flower assayed rose from 14% to 19% between 2014 and 2020 and that of concentrates from 46% to 68%. They describe the median of 12% studied as well below what is currently on the market and say the low strengths studied are likely due to the restriction of research cannabis in the United States to a federal supply that lacks concentrates.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors write that most studies failed to capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose, and recommend that studies at least report THC concentration, product used, frequency of use and route, in THC units that can be standardised. They state that THC concentration is not the same as dose.

evidence.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding and interests in the included studies: 24% (109) did not report a funding source and 32% (143) did not report whether authors had conflicts of interest; 25 studies (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author who disclosed a financial tie with the industry.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Limitations, paragraph; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Conclusions: the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace; there are serious limitations in the generalisability of the studies to the current marketplace or to the people who buy its products; high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce. Limits: searches were sensitive rather than specific; relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening; heterogeneity of designs did not allow risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies; incomplete and inconsistent reporting left gaps in the extracted data.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph; Conflicts of Interest, paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph (PMC shows it under the Plain-Language Summary heading as its 3rd paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Funded by the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317, which asked the Colorado School of Public Health for a review of the physical and mental health effects of high-potency THC marijuana and concentrates; the funder was not involved in the design, conduct or publication of the paper. As printed: one author is a paid consultant as conflict-of-interest advisor for Health Canada, including its cannabis committees; one is a paid author for UpToDate for a chapter on cannabis intoxication; one has research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research (Colorado State University) and serves on the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed.

risk_of_bias.note: Field study (Bidwell 2020): ROBINS-E overall high; confounding and selection each high (self-chosen form, groups differing in concentrate days, years of regular use and baseline THC metabolite; volunteers who had used the strongest product before; 12 people left out by their post-use blood THC), no placebo, thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold, near-threshold results described inconsistently. Scoping review (Bero 2023): AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), mainly because it does not assess bias in the studies it maps; it extracts no results.

inconsistency.note: One field study; the review reports no results to compare with it. Not assessable.

indirectness.note: Regular consumers who had used the strongest assigned product before without a bad reaction, one dispensary in one state, one session of free use, blood measured about 13 minutes and 1 hour after use; impairment inferred from change in the same people without a placebo; the review's counts concern studies, not health effects.

imprecision.note: 121 people, 26 to 33 in each strength group; the reported null form effects (intoxication, recall, balance) come from a study not designed to show equivalence and give no confidence intervals; results at P = .02 and P = .05 are unresolved.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one field study.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The field study randomised labelled strength within each form but not the form, so the concentrate-against-flower comparison that this claim reports is observational. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high (self-chosen form with baseline differences in concentrate use, years of regular use and THC metabolite; selected volunteers; no placebo or no-use session; exclusion of 12 people by an outcome; thirteen outcomes at a fixed threshold). The scoping review adds counts of what has been studied and no results, and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (provisional: the appendix was not read) chiefly because it does not appraise the studies it maps. Indirectness -1: regular consumers, one dispensary, one session, blood at about 13 minutes and 1 hour, impairment inferred without a placebo. Imprecision -1: 121 people, 26 to 33 per strength group, no confidence intervals, null form effects from a study not built to show equivalence, results at P = .02 and P = .05 unresolved. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one field study. Worded as 'is associated with' because each person chose the form and the groups differed at baseline; the statement of what the scoping review found is a statement about the literature, not about health effects.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one field study of 121 regular consumers (Bidwell 2020: one group of researchers, one state, one session, follow-up one hour; registered as NCT03522103, protocol and supplement not read, so strength results are as the main text reports them) and one scoping review that maps studies and extracts no results (Bero 2023: AMSTAR 2 provisional; appendix, evidence map and OSF protocol not read). Petrilli 2022 (cannabis potency and mental ill health and addiction, systematic review) is not yet readable and will be added: this claim says nothing about dependence or mental-health outcomes of concentrates. No cannabis-industry funding is printed for either paper, so there is no industry-funded finding to pair; the review counts that 6% of the studies it maps were industry-funded and 13% had an author with an industry tie. Both papers draw on money or advice from the Colorado state health department (Bidwell: its grant; Bero: state funding under House Bill 21-1317 and an author on the department's advisory committee): a reason to read closely, not to discount. Strengths, amounts and times appear only as study conditions or measured content (labelled strength, grams used, minutes after use); none appears in the plain wording. The 'strong conclusions' wording in Bero's Abstract refers to the usefulness of the literature, not to health effects.
